questions.q: An opportunistic infection is one that:
o: Affects only people who travel abroad
Is always caused by HIV itself
Is caused by microbes that rarely harm people with a healthy immune system
questions.x: Opportunistic microbes are normally kept in check by the immune system; they cause disease when immunity is weak, as in AIDS.

questions.q: Outside the body HIV survives poorly. It is readily destroyed by:
o: Exposure to normal room air for a few seconds only
questions.x: HIV's lipid envelope is fragile, so heat, drying and disinfectants such as bleach inactivate it. Antibiotics act on bacteria and have no effect on viruses.

questions.q: When one pyruvate molecule is oxidized completely through the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, how many carbon dioxide molecules are released?
questions.x: One carbon dioxide is lost in the link reaction and two more in one turn of the Krebs cycle, so all three carbons of pyruvate leave as carbon dioxide.

questions.q: How many molecules of oxygen are needed to oxidize one molecule of glucose completely?
questions.x: The overall equation is C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. So six molecules of oxygen are used for every molecule of glucose.

questions.q: Under normal conditions, human brain cells depend mainly on which respiratory fuel?
questions.x: The brain normally respires glucose almost exclusively, which is why blood glucose must be kept steady.

questions.q: By its shape, the enzyme amylase is classified as a:
o: Fibrous protein, forming long insoluble strands
Globular protein, folded into a compact rounded shape
questions.x: Enzymes such as amylase are globular proteins: compact, folded and usually water-soluble. Fibrous proteins, such as keratin, form long strands with structural roles.

questions.q: DNA is a polymer whose monomers are:
questions.x: DNA is a polynucleotide: a long chain of nucleotides. Amino acids build proteins, and a nucleosome is DNA wound around histones.

questions.q: Which statement about hydrogen ions in an aqueous solution is correct?
o: A rise in H⁺ concentration raises the pH
A rise in H⁺ concentration lowers the pH
H⁺ ions do not affect pH
Pure water contains no H⁺ ions at all
questions.x: pH is a measure of H⁺ concentration on a reverse scale, so more H⁺ means a lower pH (more acidic). Pure water does contain a small amount of H⁺ from ionization.

questions.q: An mRNA reads AUG GCA UUU UAG. How many tRNA molecules pair with its codons during translation?
questions.x: AUG, GCA and UUU each pair with a tRNA carrying an amino acid. UAG is a stop codon with no matching tRNA, so only three tRNAs are used.

questions.q: The amylose part of starch forms:
o: A straight chain of β-glucose units joined by β(1→4) bonds
A highly branched chain with α(1→6) links every few units
A helical (coiled) chain of α-glucose units joined by α(1→4) bonds
questions.x: Amylose is an unbranched chain of α-glucose with α(1→4) links that winds into a helix. Straight β(1→4) chains are cellulose, and heavy branching is typical of glycogen.

questions.q: Haemoglobin contains a total of 574 amino acids in its four polypeptide chains. How many peptide bonds does the molecule contain?
questions.x: Each chain has one fewer peptide bond than its number of amino acids. With four separate chains, the total is 574 − 4 = 570.

questions.q: A single hydrogen bond is weak, yet hydrogen bonding gives water many special properties. This is because:
o: Each hydrogen bond is stronger than a covalent bond
Very large numbers of hydrogen bonds form together, even though each lasts only a short time
Hydrogen bonds never break once formed
Hydrogen bonds form only in ice, never in liquid water
questions.x: Individually weak, hydrogen bonds act together in enormous numbers, so they have a large combined effect on properties such as specific heat and cohesion. In liquid water they constantly break and re-form.

questions.q: When a chloride ion (Cl⁻) dissolves in water, the surrounding water molecules turn so that:
o: Their oxygen atoms face the ion
They form covalent bonds with the ion
They move away and leave the ion bare
Their hydrogen atoms face the ion
questions.x: The negative chloride ion attracts the partly positive hydrogen ends of water molecules. Positive ions such as Na⁺ attract the partly negative oxygen ends instead.

questions.q: A codon never stands for two different amino acids. This feature of the code is called:
questions.x: Unambiguous means a codon never stands for two different amino acids. The reverse is not true: most amino acids have several codons (degeneracy).

questions.q: A triglyceride in which all three fatty acids are of the same kind is called a:
questions.x: When the three fatty acids are identical the triglyceride is simple; when they differ it is mixed. Phospholipids have a phosphate group and waxes contain no glycerol.

questions.q: Compared with monosaccharides and disaccharides, polysaccharides are generally:
o: Tasteless and mostly insoluble in water
Small molecules that pass easily through membranes
questions.x: Polysaccharides are huge molecules, so they are not sweet and most are insoluble, which suits them for storage and structure. Simple sugars are sweet, soluble and crystalline.

questions.q: In the cell cycle, chromosomes replicate their DNA during the:
questions.x: DNA is copied in the S (synthesis) phase, so each chromosome enters mitosis as two sister chromatids.

questions.q: Chromosomes become clearly visible under a light microscope:
o: During cell division, when the chromatin condenses
questions.x: In interphase the chromatin is long and thin; during cell division it coils up into thick, short chromosomes that can be seen and counted.

questions.q: In a nucleus at interphase, the genetic material appears as a network of fine threads called:
questions.x: Between divisions DNA and its proteins are spread out as a fine chromatin network. Chromatids are the condensed halves of a replicated chromosome seen during division.

questions.q: In the Gram stain, Gram-positive bacteria appear:
o: Pink, because they lose the crystal violet stain
Colourless, because they take up no stain
Purple, because their thick peptidoglycan wall keeps the crystal violet stain
questions.x: Thick peptidoglycan in Gram-positive walls holds the crystal violet–iodine complex, so they stay purple. Gram-negative bacteria lose it and take up the pink counterstain.

questions.q: Prokaryotic organisms such as bacteria and cyanobacteria are placed in the kingdom:
questions.x: All prokaryotes are grouped in kingdom Monera, also called Prokaryotae. Protists, fungi and plants are all eukaryotic.

questions.q: In the coughing reflex, the receptors that are stimulated lie in the:
o: Lining of the larynx and trachea
questions.x: Coughing begins when irritants stimulate receptors in the lining of the air passages such as the larynx and trachea. The diaphragm and other breathing muscles are effectors, not receptors.

questions.q: Nissl's granules are found in the cell body of a neuron but not in its axon. Therefore proteins needed by the axon must be:
o: Made by ribosomes spread throughout the axon
Absorbed from tissue fluid around the axon
Made at the nodes of Ranvier
Made in the cell body and carried along the axon
questions.x: Nissl's granules (rough ER and ribosomes) are the protein-making sites. Since the axon lacks them, its proteins are made in the cell body and transported down the axon.

questions.q: The integrating centre of the reflex that narrows the pupil in bright light lies in the:
questions.x: The pupil reflex is coordinated in the midbrain, which contains centres for visual reflexes. The occipital lobe is where light is consciously seen, but the reflex does not need it.

questions.q: A reflex arc contains a sensory neuron, a chain of three interneurons and a motor neuron. How many synapses between neurons are present in this arc?
questions.x: Five neurons joined end to end have four junctions between them: sensory to first interneuron, two between interneurons, and last interneuron to motor neuron. The junction with the effector is not a synapse between neurons.

questions.q: Side branches given off along the length of an axon are called:
questions.x: Collaterals are branches of the axon itself and conduct impulses away from the cell body. Dendrites are separate processes of the cell body.

questions.q: The dorsal root ganglion, a small swelling on the dorsal root of each spinal nerve, is part of the reflex pathway. It contains the:
o: Synapses between sensory and motor neurons
questions.x: The dorsal root ganglion holds the cell bodies of the sensory (afferent) neurons. Motor neuron cell bodies, interneurons and the synapses of the arc all lie in the grey matter of the spinal cord.

questions.q: Releasing hormones made by the hypothalamus act directly on the:
questions.x: Hypothalamic releasing hormones travel in blood vessels to the anterior pituitary and control its secretions. The posterior pituitary instead stores hormones made by the hypothalamus itself.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of events in non-competitive inhibition?
o: Substrate binds → inhibitor joins the active site → products form → enzyme is freed
Inhibitor binds the active site → substrate is displaced → enzyme is denatured → products form
Active site is distorted → inhibitor binds at another site → enzyme changes shape → substrate is converted
Inhibitor binds at another site → enzyme changes shape → active site is distorted → substrate is not converted
questions.x: The non-competitive inhibitor first binds away from the active site; the resulting shape change distorts the active site so the substrate cannot be converted.

questions.q: In feedback inhibition, the end product can inhibit the first enzyme of the pathway even though it has a different shape from that enzyme's substrate. This is possible because:
o: It binds at a separate allosteric site, not the active site
It has exactly the same shape as the substrate
It increases the amount of substrate
questions.x: The end product does not compete for the active site. It binds a regulatory (allosteric) site, which changes the shape of the active site.

questions.q: Sulpha drugs (sulphonamides) have a shape very like PABA, a substance bacteria use to make folic acid. These drugs act on the bacterial enzyme as:
questions.x: A molecule that resembles the substrate and competes with it for the active site is a competitive inhibitor.

questions.q: A few RNA molecules can also catalyse chemical reactions. Such catalytic RNA molecules are called:
questions.x: Ribozymes are RNA molecules with catalytic activity; they are the main exception to the rule that enzymes are proteins. An apoenzyme is the protein part of a conjugated enzyme.

questions.q: Which of the following does NOT denature an enzyme?
questions.x: Low temperature only slows an enzyme, and activity returns on warming. Heat and extremes of pH destroy its three-dimensional shape.

questions.q: Darwin noticed that the animals of the Galápagos Islands most closely resembled those of:
questions.x: Galápagos species were similar to, but different from, those of nearby South America. Darwin concluded they descended from mainland colonists and changed after reaching the islands.

questions.q: Free oxygen first started to build up in the atmosphere only after:
o: Photosynthetic prokaryotes had been releasing it for a long time
questions.x: Photosynthetic prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria released oxygen. At first it reacted with iron and other substances, so free oxygen built up only gradually. Ozone, eukaryotes and animals followed later.

questions.q: A trait that is fixed by genes at fertilisation, and NOT gained during life, is:
o: A scar left by a deep cut
Strong leg muscles of a regular runner
The ABO blood group of a person
A tanned skin from working in sunlight
questions.x: The ABO blood group is fixed by the alleles inherited from the parents. Scars, trained muscles and a suntan develop during life and are acquired.

questions.q: Inside a helper T cell, the DNA copy of the HIV genome:
o: Is inserted into the host cell's own DNA
Is broken down immediately by the host
Is released from the cell as free DNA
Is converted into protein without transcription
questions.x: Viral DNA made by reverse transcriptase is integrated into the host chromosome as a provirus. It can stay hidden for years and later direct new virus production.

questions.q: In a regular 28-day cycle, the proliferative phase of the uterus lasts roughly from:
questions.x: Days 1–5 are menstruation; the endometrium then rebuilds (proliferative phase) until ovulation at about day 14. The secretory phase follows.

questions.q: Testosterone, oestrogen and progesterone all belong to which chemical class of hormones?
questions.x: The sex hormones are steroids made from cholesterol. FSH and LH, by contrast, are glycoproteins.

questions.q: How many chromosomes does a human spermatid contain?
questions.x: Spermatids are formed by meiosis II, so they are haploid with 23 chromosomes (22 autosomes and one sex chromosome).

questions.q: A man's blood test shows a raised uric acid level, but he has never had joint pain. Which statement is correct?
o: He must already have advanced osteoarthritis
He has rheumatoid arthritis, because uric acid attacks the synovial membrane
A raised uric acid level always causes immediate joint pain
Gout arises only when urate crystals deposit in joints, so a high level alone may cause no symptoms
questions.x: Gout attacks happen when urate crystals are deposited in a joint and inflame it; a raised level without crystals can be symptom-free. Raised uric acid is not a sign of osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.q: The muscle in the walls of arteries that narrows them during vasoconstriction is:
questions.x: The middle layer of an artery wall contains smooth muscle, which contracts involuntarily to narrow the vessel. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.

questions.q: A myofibril has 1000 sarcomeres in series. Each shortens from 2.5 µm to 2.0 µm. By how much does the myofibril shorten?
questions.x: Each sarcomere shortens by 0.5 µm, so the total is 1000 × 0.5 µm = 500 µm = 0.5 mm. The answer 0.5 µm is the change in a single sarcomere only.

questions.q: The joints between the tarsal bones of the ankle region, which let flat bone surfaces slide slightly over each other, are:
questions.x: Like the joints between carpal bones, intertarsal joints have flat surfaces that slide a little over one another, which makes them gliding (plane) joints.

questions.q: Lactic acid formed in skeletal muscle during vigorous exercise is mostly carried by the blood to the:
o: Lungs, where it is breathed out
Liver, where it is converted back to pyruvate or glucose
questions.x: The liver takes up lactic acid and turns it back into pyruvate and glucose, using oxygen taken in during recovery. Lactic acid is not exhaled and is not stored in the spleen.

questions.q: The thoracic and lumbar regions of the human vertebral column contain, respectively:
questions.x: There are 12 thoracic vertebrae, one for each pair of ribs, and 5 large lumbar vertebrae in the lower back. Seven is the number of cervical vertebrae.

questions.q: A child's diet lacks vitamin D for a long time. The bones become soft and the legs bow because:
o: Too little calcium is absorbed to mineralise the bone matrix
No collagen can be made in the bones
Red marrow is replaced by yellow marrow
The cartilage at the joints becomes calcified
questions.x: Vitamin D is needed to absorb calcium from the gut. Without it the bone matrix is poorly mineralised and stays soft (rickets), so weight-bearing bones bend.

questions.q: Which pairing of a form of arthritis with its main cause is correct?
o: Osteoarthritis — immune attack on the joint lining
Gout — deposition of urate crystals in joints
Rheumatoid arthritis — high uric acid in the blood
Septic arthritis — gradual wear of cartilage with age
questions.x: Gout is caused by urate crystal deposition. Immune attack is the cause of rheumatoid arthritis, wear with age of osteoarthritis, and infection of septic arthritis.

questions.q: A boy has an X-linked allele. Which of these relatives could NOT have passed this allele to him?
questions.x: A boy's only X comes from his mother, who got it from either of her parents. His father gave him a Y, so nothing X-linked can reach him from the father's side.

questions.q: Which cross is used to find out whether genes A and B are linked?
o: A test cross of the dihybrid with a double recessive
A cross between two double homozygous dominants
A cross of the dihybrid with a double homozygous dominant
A cross between two double recessives
questions.x: Crossing AaBb with aabb shows the gametes of the dihybrid directly. Equal classes mean independent assortment; excess parental classes mean linkage.

questions.q: Looking at seed colour alone among the plants of a dihybrid F2 (RrYy selfed), the genotypes YY, Yy and yy occur in the ratio:
questions.x: Each gene in a dihybrid cross still follows the monohybrid pattern, so Yy × Yy gives 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy. The 3 : 1 is the phenotypic ratio for colour.

questions.q: The garden pea has 2n = 14. How many linkage groups does it have?
questions.x: The number of linkage groups equals the haploid number. With 2n = 14, n = 7, so peas have 7 linkage groups.

questions.q: Chiasmata move towards the ends of the chromosomes (terminalisation). This is completed in which substage of prophase I?
questions.x: Terminalisation of chiasmata is completed in diakinesis, the last substage of prophase I. Chiasmata become visible in diplotene, after crossing over in pachytene.

questions.q: The most common form of hemophilia is:
o: Hemophilia B, due to lack of factor IX
Hemophilia B, due to lack of factor VIII
Hemophilia A, due to lack of factor VIII
Hemophilia A, due to lack of platelets
questions.x: Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) makes up most cases. Hemophilia B, or Christmas disease, is due to factor IX deficiency and is less common.

questions.q: In his F2 for seed shape, Mendel counted 5474 round and 1850 wrinkled seeds. These numbers are closest to the ratio:
questions.x: 5474 ÷ 1850 is about 2.96, which is very close to 3 : 1, the monohybrid F2 phenotypic ratio. 1 : 2 : 1 is the genotypic ratio, not the phenotypic one.

questions.q: Because it appeared in several European ruling families, hemophilia is often called:
questions.x: Hemophilia spread through many European royal families from Queen Victoria, who was a carrier, so it became known as the royal disease.

questions.q: Comparing the two normal heart sounds, the first sound 'lubb' is:
o: Longer and lower in pitch than 'dubb'
Produced while the ventricles are relaxed
questions.x: 'Lubb' is the longer, low-pitched sound of the atrioventricular valves closing. 'Dubb' is shorter and sharper, from the semilunar valves closing.

questions.q: The superior vena cava brings deoxygenated blood to the heart from the:
questions.x: The superior vena cava drains the upper part of the body: head, neck and arms. Blood from the lower body comes through the inferior vena cava, and from the lungs through the pulmonary veins.

questions.q: Each day, the lymphatic system returns to the blood about:
o: A few litres (about 3 litres) of fluid
questions.x: Of the fluid that leaves the blood capillaries daily, roughly 3 litres is not reabsorbed and is returned by the lymph vessels.

questions.q: Lymph from all over the body is finally collected into two large vessels, the:
o: Hepatic portal vein and thoracic duct
Thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct
questions.x: Lymph vessels join to form two main ducts, the thoracic duct and the right lymphatic duct, which empty lymph into the veins near the neck.

questions.q: Which of these white blood cells attacks every invader in the same way, and so does NOT take part in specific defence?
questions.x: Neutrophils are phagocytes that attack any invader in the same way, so they are part of non-specific defence. Plasma cells, helper T cells and memory B cells all act against particular antigens.

questions.q: Antibodies are also known as:
questions.x: Antibodies are immunoglobulins (Ig), proteins such as IgG and IgM. Antigens are the foreign molecules that antibodies bind.

questions.q: Louis Pasteur is known for developing a vaccine against:
questions.x: Pasteur developed vaccines against rabies and anthrax. Jenner's work was on smallpox, Salk and Sabin made polio vaccines, and BCG is for tuberculosis.

questions.q: The glottis is:
o: The leaf-shaped flap of cartilage above the larynx
The opening between the vocal cords in the larynx
The point where the trachea divides into two bronchi
The passage joining the nasal cavity to the pharynx
questions.x: The glottis is the slit-like opening between the vocal cords through which air enters the trachea. The flap that covers it during swallowing is the epiglottis, a different structure.

questions.q: At its lower end, the trachea divides into:
o: Many bronchioles that open straight into alveoli
Three bronchi, one for each lobe of the right lung
Two alveolar ducts, one for each lung
Two primary bronchi, one going to each lung
questions.x: The trachea branches into a right and a left primary (main) bronchus, one for each lung. These then branch further inside the lungs into smaller bronchi and bronchioles.

questions.q: A boy with a blocked nose breathes only through his mouth for several days. Compared with nose breathing, the air reaching his trachea is:
o: Richer in oxygen and lower in carbon dioxide
Exactly the same, because the pharynx does all the conditioning
Cooler, drier and less well filtered
questions.x: The nasal cavity, with its hairs, mucus and rich blood supply, cleans, warms and moistens air. The mouth does this far less, so mouth-breathed air is cooler, drier and dirtier. Its oxygen content is unchanged.

questions.q: Gastric glands in the stomach wall pour their secretions into the stomach through tiny openings in its lining called:
questions.x: The stomach mucosa is dotted with gastric pits, into which the gastric glands open. Rugae are the large folds of the empty stomach, and villi and crypts belong to the small intestine.

questions.q: Heartburn, a burning pain behind the breastbone, occurs when:
o: Acidic stomach contents pass back into the oesophagus through a weak cardiac sphincter
Bile flows back into the liver
Pepsin digests the wall of the colon
Food enters the trachea instead of the oesophagus
questions.x: The cardiac sphincter normally stops stomach contents rising. If it is weak, acid refluxes into the oesophagus, whose lining lacks the stomach's thick mucus protection, causing a burning feeling. It has nothing to do with the heart.

questions.q: For long-term haemodialysis, a surgeon often joins an artery to a vein in the patient's arm. This is done to:
o: Make a large, strong blood vessel that can be used again and again
questions.x: Joining an artery to a vein (a fistula) enlarges the vein so needles can be inserted repeatedly and blood can flow fast enough to and from the machine.

questions.q: Snakes and lizards are slow and sluggish on cold mornings because:
o: They have used up all their stored fat
Their hypothalamus switches off at night
Their low body temperature slows their enzyme-controlled metabolism
questions.x: Ectotherms take up the temperature of their surroundings, and at low temperature their enzymes work slowly, so muscle activity is slow.

questions.q: Calcium phosphate stones are more likely to form when the urine is:
questions.x: Calcium phosphate is less soluble in alkaline urine, so it crystallises more easily there. Dilute urine and absence of calcium would prevent it.

questions.q: A fall in a person's glomerular filtration rate (GFR) means that:
o: More urine is being produced each minute
The kidneys are reabsorbing more glucose
Less plasma is being filtered by the kidneys each minute
questions.x: GFR is the volume of plasma filtered per minute. A falling GFR is the key sign that kidney function is declining; a rise in glomerular pressure would increase it.

questions.q: Which substance is NOT normally added to the tubular fluid by tubular secretion?
questions.x: Hydrogen ions, potassium ions and some drugs are secreted from the blood into the tubule. Glucose moves the other way: it is filtered and then completely reabsorbed.

questions.q: Animals whose body temperature changes with the temperature of their surroundings are called:
questions.x: Poikilotherms have a variable body temperature; homeotherms keep it constant. Heterotroph refers to nutrition, not temperature.

questions.q: In kidney failure, a high level of potassium in the blood is dangerous mainly because it can:
o: Cause stones in the gall bladder
Disturb the rhythm of the heart
questions.x: Healthy kidneys excrete excess potassium. When it builds up, it upsets the electrical activity of heart muscle and can cause dangerous rhythms.

questions.q: Each kidney is enclosed in a tough, fibrous outer covering called the:
questions.x: The renal capsule is the protective fibrous coat around the whole kidney. Bowman's capsule is a tiny cup at the start of each nephron, and the cortex lies just inside the renal capsule.

questions.q: A major advantage of being an endotherm is that the animal:
o: Can remain active in cold conditions when ectotherms are sluggish
Needs less food than an ectotherm of the same size
Never loses heat to the surroundings
questions.x: A steady, warm body temperature keeps enzymes working at a high rate whatever the weather. The cost is that endotherms need more food.

questions.q: Starting from one double-stranded DNA molecule, what is the smallest number of PCR cycles needed to obtain at least 1000 copies of the target?
questions.x: The amount doubles every cycle, giving 2ⁿ copies after n cycles. 2⁹ = 512 is too few, while 2¹⁰ = 1024 is the first value above 1000.

questions.q: The first product of recombinant DNA technology approved for treating humans, in 1982, was:
questions.x: Human insulin made by genetically engineered E. coli was approved in 1982, the first recombinant medicine. tPA, erythropoietin and recombinant clotting factors followed later.

questions.q: A rare risk of the oral (Sabin) polio vaccine is that:
o: It contains toxins that damage the liver
It makes people allergic to all other vaccines
The weakened virus may mutate back to a form that can cause paralysis
It causes antibodies to attack the person's own nerves
questions.x: Because the oral vaccine contains live attenuated virus, in very rare cases the virus mutates and regains its ability to cause paralysis. This risk does not exist with the inactivated (Salk) vaccine.

questions.q: In PCR, DNA polymerase cannot start making a new strand without a primer because it:
o: Can only add nucleotides to the free 3' end of an existing strand
Is destroyed at the annealing temperature
Needs the primer as an energy source
questions.x: DNA polymerase extends an existing chain by adding nucleotides to its 3' end; it cannot begin a chain from nothing. The primers provide these starting 3' ends on each side of the target.

questions.q: How many moles of nitrogen gas are present in 5.6 dm³ of N₂ at STP? (1 mol of gas at STP = 22.4 dm³)
questions.x: Moles = volume ÷ molar volume = 5.6 ÷ 22.4 = 0.25 mol. 4.0 mol comes from dividing the wrong way round.

questions.q: For 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, what is the theoretical yield of magnesium oxide from 4.8 g of magnesium burnt in excess oxygen? (Mg = 24, O = 16)
questions.x: Mg = 4.8/24 = 0.2 mol; ratio Mg : MgO = 1 : 1, so 0.2 mol MgO × 40 = 8.0 g. 4.0 g wrongly halves the moles using the coefficient 2.

questions.q: The number of electrons in the third shell (n = 3) of an iron atom (Z = 26) is:
questions.x: Fe is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s². The third shell holds 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ = 14 electrons.

questions.q: An electron occupies a 3d orbital. Its four quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) could be:
questions.x: For 3d, n = 3 and l = 2, so m can be −2 to +2. l = 3 is not allowed when n = 3, l = 1 would be a p orbital, and m = +3 is impossible when l = 2.

questions.q: Each shell has only one s orbital. This is because for l = 0:
o: The spin quantum number has only one value
The magnetic quantum number has only one value, m = 0
The principal quantum number must be 1
The magnetic quantum number has three values
questions.x: When l = 0, m can only be 0, so there is one orientation. A sphere looks the same in every direction, so one s orbital fits this.

questions.q: Which statement about absolute zero is correct?
o: It is easily reached by cooling helium gas
It is the temperature at which water freezes
It is the lowest temperature only for ideal gases, not for other substances
It has never been reached, although temperatures very close to it have been achieved
questions.x: Absolute zero (0 K) is the lowest possible temperature for all matter. It has never actually been reached, though scientists have come within a tiny fraction of a kelvin.

questions.q: The pressure of a gas is increased at constant temperature. The mean free path of its molecules:
o: Decreases, because the molecules are closer together
Increases, because the molecules move faster
Stays the same, because the temperature is constant
Increases, because there are fewer collisions
questions.x: Higher pressure at constant temperature packs the molecules closer, so a molecule travels a shorter distance before its next collision. The average speed is unchanged because the temperature is unchanged.

questions.q: A gas in a sealed rigid container is cooled. Which of the following does NOT decrease?
o: The average speed of the molecules
The number of collisions with the walls per second
The number of molecules in the container
questions.x: The container is sealed, so the number of molecules stays the same. Cooling slows the molecules, so they hit the walls less often and less hard, and the pressure falls.

questions.q: In autumn, as the surface water of a lake cools from 10 °C towards 4 °C, it:
o: Becomes less dense and stays at the surface
Freezes at once into a layer of ice
Stays at the same density and does not move
Becomes denser and sinks, so warmer water rises to the surface
questions.x: Above 4 °C, water gets denser as it cools, so cold surface water sinks and warmer water rises, until the whole lake reaches about 4 °C.

questions.q: Ammonia (NH₃) boils at a much higher temperature than phosphine (PH₃) because:
o: PH₃ molecules are lighter than NH₃ molecules
NH₃ molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds
PH₃ molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds
NH₃ has stronger London forces than PH₃
questions.x: N is small and highly electronegative, so NH₃ molecules hydrogen-bond; P is not, so PH₃ has no hydrogen bonds. PH₃ (34) is actually heavier than NH₃ (17).

questions.q: Iodine is a solid at room temperature but chlorine is a gas, although both are non-polar molecular substances. The reason is that:
o: I₂ molecules are held by hydrogen bonds
I₂ molecules are larger and more polarisable, so London forces between them are stronger
The I–I covalent bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond
Iodine forms an ionic lattice of I⁺ and I⁻ ions
questions.x: London dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons and size of the molecule. The I–I bond is actually weaker than Cl–Cl, so bond strength is not the reason.

questions.q: Which Group II oxide has the largest magnitude of lattice energy?
questions.x: All have the same 2+ and 2− charges, so the smallest cation, Mg²⁺, gives the shortest interionic distance and the strongest attraction.

questions.q: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at equilibrium, [N₂O₄] = 0.1 and [NO₂] = 0.2 mol dm⁻³. The value of Kc is:
questions.x: Kc = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄] = (0.2)²/0.1 = 0.04/0.1 = 0.4 mol dm⁻³. Forgetting the square gives 2.

questions.q: For a reaction mixture, the reaction quotient Qc is found to be greater than Kc. The mixture will:
o: Undergo net forward reaction until Qc rises to Kc
Stay unchanged, as it is already at equilibrium
Change its Kc value to match Qc
Undergo net reverse reaction until Qc falls to Kc
questions.x: Qc > Kc means there are too many products for equilibrium, so net reverse reaction occurs. Kc is fixed at a given temperature.

questions.q: When the concentration of reactant X is made three times as great, the rate of reaction becomes 27 times as great. The order with respect to X is:
questions.x: 3ⁿ = 27 gives n = 3. An order of 2 would give only 9 times the rate.

questions.q: The rate constant k is also known as the:
questions.x: k is called the specific rate constant or velocity constant; it equals the rate when every reactant concentration is unity. The equilibrium constant is a different quantity.

questions.q: On a graph of the concentration of a product against time, the curve:
o: Rises steeply at first and then levels off as the reaction slows
Falls steeply at first and then levels off
Rises more and more steeply as time passes
questions.x: Product forms fastest at the start, when reactant concentrations are highest; as reactants are used up, the slope decreases and the curve flattens.

questions.q: In thermodynamics, a spontaneous process is one that:
o: Takes place only when energy is supplied continuously
Takes place on its own, without continuous help from outside
Never reaches a state of equilibrium
questions.x: A spontaneous process proceeds by itself once conditions allow. Spontaneity says nothing about speed: some spontaneous changes are very slow.

questions.q: The standard enthalpy of formation of ammonia corresponds to which reaction?
questions.x: Formation means 1 mol of compound from its elements in their standard states. N₂ + 3H₂ gives 2 mol, and N(g), H(g) atoms are not standard states.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of carbon in methanal, HCHO?
questions.x: 2(+1) + x + (−2) = 0, so x = 0. Carbon in organic compounds can have zero oxidation number even though it is bonded to other atoms.

questions.q: When a zinc rod is dipped in a solution of zinc ions, an electrode potential develops mainly because:
o: Zinc ions from the solution always deposit on the rod and make it positive
The rod dissolves completely in the solution
Some zinc atoms enter the solution as Zn²⁺, leaving electrons on the rod and creating a charge separation
Hydrogen gas is released at the surface of the rod
questions.x: Atoms leaving as ions leave the metal negatively charged and the nearby solution positive; this electrical double layer gives the electrode potential.

questions.q: In a sigma (σ) bond, the electron density is:
o: Concentrated along the line joining the two nuclei
Present only above and below the line joining the nuclei
Located only on the more electronegative atom
Spread evenly over the whole molecule
questions.x: A σ bond forms by head-on overlap, so electron density lies along the internuclear axis and is symmetrical around it. Density above and below the axis describes a π bond.

questions.q: Electronegativities: C 2.5, H 2.1. The C–H bond is best described as:
o: Highly polar, with H as the negative end
questions.x: An electronegativity difference of only 0.4 gives very little charge separation, so the C–H bond is nearly non-polar. This is why hydrocarbons are non-polar.

questions.q: To find the percentage ionic character of a bond, its observed dipole moment is compared with:
o: The dipole moment of the H–H bond
The bond energy of the same bond
The dipole moment calculated assuming complete transfer of an electron
questions.x: % ionic character = (observed μ ÷ μ for a fully ionic bond) × 100, where the fully ionic value assumes a whole electronic charge at each end of the bond.

questions.q: The reduction of nuclear attraction on valence electrons caused by the inner electrons is called the shielding effect. Down a group, shielding:
o: Decreases, which raises the ionisation energy
Increases, which helps lower the ionisation energy
Stays constant, so ionisation energy is unchanged
questions.x: More inner shells are present further down a group, so shielding increases and the outer electron is removed more easily.

questions.q: The d-block elements are also known as:
questions.x: The d-block lies between the s- and p-blocks and its elements are called transition elements.

questions.q: Chromium's ground-state atom is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ rather than [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s². The reason is that:
o: A half-filled 3d⁵ subshell has extra stability
The 4s orbital can hold only one electron in chromium
A completely filled 3d subshell is formed
questions.x: Moving one 4s electron into 3d gives a half-filled 3d⁵ subshell, which is especially stable. The 4s orbital can still hold two electrons, and 3d⁵ is half-filled, not full.

questions.q: Natural gas, an important source of organic compounds, consists mainly of:
questions.x: Natural gas is mostly methane, CH₄, with small amounts of ethane, propane and butane.

questions.q: Benzene and its derivatives were called 'aromatic' compounds because many of the first ones known:
o: Were very good conductors of electricity
questions.x: The name comes from the aroma of early compounds such as benzaldehyde. Today the term refers to the benzene-type ring, not the smell.

questions.q: All contributing structures of a molecule must have the same:
questions.x: Resonance structures keep every atom in the same place and differ only in electron positions. The real hybrid has lower energy than any of them.

questions.q: Sodium acetylide reacts with water to give back ethyne and sodium hydroxide. This shows that:
o: Ethyne is a stronger acid than water
Water is a weaker acid than ethane
Water is a stronger acid than ethyne
questions.x: The acetylide ion takes H⁺ from water, so water gives up its proton more easily than ethyne does. Ethyne is only a very weak acid.

questions.q: Which statement about the individual Kekulé structures of benzene is correct?
o: Neither exists on its own, so neither can be isolated
Each can be isolated at low temperature
They change into each other rapidly like two isomers
One is more stable and makes up most of a benzene sample
questions.x: Contributing structures are only ways of writing the electrons. The real benzene molecule is a single hybrid; the two Kekulé structures are equivalent and neither exists separately.

questions.q: Hydrocarbon P reacts with Br₂ to give C₂H₄Br₂ as the only product. Hydrocarbon Q reacts with Br₂ in sunlight to give C₂H₅Br and HBr. Which statement is correct?
o: P is ethane and reacts by substitution; Q is ethene and reacts by addition
Both are ethene and react by addition
P is ethyne and reacts by substitution; Q is ethene and reacts by addition
P is ethene and reacts by addition; Q is ethane and reacts by substitution
questions.x: Ethene adds Br₂ across C=C with no by-product. Ethane has no π bond, so in light a Br atom replaces an H atom, releasing HBr.

questions.q: 21.8 g of bromoethane, C₂H₅Br (M = 109), is completely converted into ethene by alcoholic KOH. What mass of ethene is formed? (C 12, H 1)
questions.x: Moles of C₂H₅Br = 21.8/109 = 0.2 mol, giving 0.2 mol C₂H₄; 0.2 × 28 = 5.6 g.

questions.q: Benzene is often drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside. The circle represents:
o: Six π electrons delocalised over all six carbon atoms
A ring of six hydrogen atoms
Six lone pairs on the carbon atoms
questions.x: The circle shows that the π electrons are not fixed in three double bonds but spread evenly round the ring. Benzene has no lone pairs on carbon.

questions.q: A student writes 2-ethylbut-2-ene as the name of CH₃CH=C(CH₂CH₃)CH₃. The correct systematic name is:
questions.x: The longest chain through the double bond includes the ethyl group, giving five carbons, not four. Numbered from the left, C=C is at carbon 2 and the methyl at carbon 3.

questions.q: When alcoholic KOH converts an alkyl halide into an alkene, the hydroxide or ethoxide ion acts as a:
o: Nucleophile, attacking the carbon bonded to the halogen
questions.x: In elimination the ion pulls off a β-hydrogen as H⁺, so it acts as a base. Attacking the carbon bonded to the halogen is its role in substitution.

questions.q: Ethanol forms an ester when heated with ethanoic acid and concentrated H₂SO₄, but phenol does not do so readily. To make phenyl ethanoate from phenol, a chemist would use:
questions.x: Phenol is a poor nucleophile because its oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so the slow acid-catalysed esterification is not used. The more reactive acid chloride gives the ester: C₆H₅OH + CH₃COCl → CH₃COOC₆H₅ + HCl.

questions.q: Propanoic acid is heated with ethanol and a little concentrated H₂SO₄. The structure of the ester formed is:
questions.x: The acid part (CH₃CH₂CO–) joins to the alkyl part of the alcohol through oxygen, giving ethyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃. CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃ is its isomer, propyl ethanoate.

questions.q: Which compound is NOT oxidised by Tollens' reagent?
questions.x: Tollens' reagent is a mild oxidising agent that oxidises aldehydes, including aromatic benzaldehyde, but not ketones. Butanone, a ketone, gives no silver mirror.

questions.q: Ethyne is passed into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate at about 80 °C. The product is:
questions.x: Water adds across the triple bond to give an unstable enol, CH₂=CHOH, which rearranges to ethanal, CH₃CHO. The Hg²⁺ ion catalyses the hydration.

questions.q: Mild, controlled oxidation of methanol gives:
questions.x: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde, so CH₃OH gives HCHO (methanal). Further oxidation would give methanoic acid.

questions.q: Oxalic acid, HOOC–COOH, has the IUPAC name:
questions.x: It has two carbons, both in –COOH groups, so it is ethanedioic acid. Ethanoic acid has only one carboxyl group.

questions.q: The tertiary structure of a protein, its overall three-dimensional folding, is held mainly by interactions between:
o: The haem groups of the protein
The side chains (R groups) of its amino acids
questions.x: Tertiary folding is held by disulphide bridges, ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic forces between R groups. Links between separate chains describe quaternary structure.

questions.q: Gum arabic, a natural adhesive used on envelopes and postage stamps, is obtained from:
questions.x: Gum arabic is a plant gum collected from acacia trees and becomes sticky when moistened. Animal bones give animal glue and milk protein gives casein glue.

questions.q: Two vectors of magnitudes P and Q point in the same direction. Their scalar product is:
questions.x: P · Q = PQ cos θ, and θ = 0° for vectors in the same direction, so cos θ = 1 and the scalar product is PQ.

questions.q: A projectile is launched with speed v at angle θ above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity throughout the flight is:
questions.x: The horizontal component at launch is v cos θ, and with no horizontal force it stays the same for the whole flight. v sin θ is the initial vertical component.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. Which pair of forces is NOT an action–reaction pair?
o: The weight of the book and the upward push of the table on the book
The push of the book on the table and the push of the table on the book
The Earth's pull on the book and the book's pull on the Earth
The Earth's pull on the table and the table's pull on the Earth
questions.x: The weight of the book and the table's push both act on the same body (the book); they balance but are not a third-law pair. Third-law pairs act on two different bodies.

questions.q: The SI unit of acceleration is:
questions.x: Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time, so its unit is (m s⁻¹) ÷ s = m s⁻². m s⁻¹ is the unit of velocity.

questions.q: The momentum of a body increases steadily from 10 kg m s⁻¹ to 30 kg m s⁻¹ in 4 s. The net force acting on it is:
questions.x: F = Δp/Δt = (30 − 10) ÷ 4 = 5 N. 10 N wrongly adds the two momenta (10 + 30 = 40) and divides by 4.

questions.q: A car moving at 30 m s⁻¹ brakes with a uniform deceleration of 5 m s⁻² until it stops. The distance it covers in the last 1 s before stopping is:
questions.x: Run the motion backwards: in the last second the car is like a body starting from rest with a = 5 m s⁻², so s = ½ × 5 × 1² = 2.5 m. 5 m forgets the ½.

questions.q: A ball is projected from level ground and lands on the same level after 4 s. Ignoring air resistance, it reached its highest point after:
questions.x: Without air resistance the path is symmetric, so the time to rise equals the time to fall. Time to the top = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 s.

questions.q: The mass of a body is halved and its speed is doubled. Its kinetic energy becomes:
questions.x: KE = ½mv². Halving m gives ×½ and doubling v gives ×4, so KE becomes ½ × 4 = 2 times.

questions.q: A drill bit becomes very hot while drilling a hole in a wall. The main reason is that:
o: Electrical energy flows directly into the bit as heat
The wall gives its own heat to the drill bit
Work done against friction is converted into internal energy
The bit gains gravitational potential energy
questions.x: The bit rubs against the wall material; the work done against friction raises the internal energy of the bit and wall, so they get hot.

questions.q: Besides energies, the efficiency of a device can also be calculated as:
questions.x: Power is energy per unit time, so for the same time interval the ratio of output to input power equals the ratio of output to input energy.

questions.q: Large angular displacements are not treated as vectors because they do not obey the:
o: Rule that a vector has a magnitude
Rule for multiplying a vector by a number
questions.x: The result of two large rotations depends on the order in which they are done, so they do not add commutatively. Only very small angular displacements behave as vectors.

questions.q: In steady flow, 3 kg of liquid enters one end of a pipe every second. If the pipe has no leaks, the mass of liquid leaving the other end every second is:
o: It depends on the pipe's length
questions.x: Mass is conserved and cannot pile up in steady flow, so the mass leaving per second equals the mass entering per second.

questions.q: A systolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg is expressed in pascals as about: (1 mmHg ≈ 133 Pa)
questions.x: 120 × 133 ≈ 16 000 Pa = 1.6 × 10⁴ Pa. The other values come from a power-of-ten slip or dividing instead of multiplying.

questions.q: The path traced out by a single fluid particle in a smooth, unchanging flow pattern is called a:
questions.x: In steady flow every particle passing a given point follows the same path, and that path is a streamline. An eddy is a swirl found in turbulent flow; an isobar joins points of equal pressure.

questions.q: After an earthquake, transverse seismic waves (S-waves) are not detected on the far side of the Earth, but longitudinal waves (P-waves) are. This suggests that part of the Earth's core is:
questions.x: Transverse waves need a medium that resists sideways (shear) deformation, which a liquid cannot do, while longitudinal waves pass through liquids. Empty space would block the P-waves as well.

questions.q: A thicker string has 4 times the mass per unit length of a thinner one. Both have the same length and tension. The fundamental frequency of the thicker string is:
o: Twice that of the thinner string
One quarter that of the thinner string
The same as that of the thinner string
Half that of the thinner string
questions.x: f = (1/2L)√(T/μ), so f ∝ 1/√μ. Four times the mass per unit length gives half the frequency.

questions.q: The speed of sound in air at −73 °C is 280 m s⁻¹. At 527 °C it will be:
questions.x: In kelvin the temperatures are 200 K and 800 K, a ratio of 4. Since v ∝ √T, the speed doubles to 560 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 1120.

questions.q: Two progressive waves, each of frequency 200 Hz, travel in opposite directions on a string and form a stationary wave. The particles at an antinode vibrate with a frequency of:
questions.x: Superposition does not change frequency: every particle of the stationary wave, including those at antinodes, vibrates at the frequency of the component waves.

questions.q: In a stationary wave, the distance from the first antinode to the fifth antinode is 80 cm. The wavelength is:
questions.x: Adjacent antinodes are λ/2 apart, and from the first to the fifth there are 4 gaps: 4 × λ/2 = 80 cm, so λ = 40 cm.

questions.q: The energy carried by a progressive wave moves through the medium at:
o: The maximum speed of the particles
Zero speed, since energy stays at the source
The speed of light, whatever the wave
questions.x: Energy is handed on from particle to particle as the disturbance advances, so it travels at the wave speed v = fλ. Particle speed is a different quantity.

questions.q: A particle's SHM is modelled by a point going round a circle once every 1.2 s. Starting from the middle of its path, how long does the particle take to reach an extreme position?
questions.x: Going from the centre to one end corresponds to a quarter turn of the reference point, so it takes T/4 = 1.2/4 = 0.3 s.

questions.q: A piston does 150 J of work compressing a gas, and meanwhile the gas loses 150 J as heat through the cylinder walls. What happens to its internal energy?
questions.x: Energy gained as work (+150 J) equals energy lost as heat (−150 J), so ΔU = +150 − 150 = 0 and the temperature of an ideal gas stays the same.

questions.q: The internal energy of a system is the:
o: Kinetic energy of the system moving as a whole
Heat that the system has given out
Sum of the kinetic and potential energies of all its molecules
Work done on the system by gravity
questions.x: Internal energy is the total of the random kinetic energies and the intermolecular potential energies of the molecules, not the motion of the whole body.

questions.q: In a uniform electric field of 5000 V m⁻¹, what is the potential difference between two points 3 mm apart measured along the field direction?
questions.x: In a uniform field V = Ed = 5000 × 3 × 10⁻³ = 15 V. Treating mm as cm gives 150 V; dividing gives a huge wrong value.

questions.q: A capacitor charged to 10 V discharges through a resistor. Taking e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37, the voltage across it after one time constant is about:
questions.x: During discharge, after one time constant the voltage falls to about 37% of its initial value: 0.37 × 10 = 3.7 V. 6.3 V is the value reached after one time constant of charging.

questions.q: A big metal sheet's charge per unit area is made two times bigger. What happens to the field strength right next to its surface?
questions.x: E = σ/ε₀ is directly proportional to σ, so doubling σ doubles the field.

questions.q: A source of internal resistance 1 Ω is connected to a 3 Ω load. The efficiency of power transfer to the load is:
questions.x: Efficiency = R ÷ (R + r) = 3 ÷ 4 = 75%. The other 25% is dissipated inside the source; 50% applies only when R = r.

questions.q: A steady current of 0.8 A flows through a lamp for 5 minutes. The number of electrons that pass through it is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C):
questions.x: Q = It = 0.8 × 300 = 240 C. n = Q/e = 240 ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5 × 10²¹. Using 5 s instead of 300 s gives 2.5 × 10¹⁹.

questions.q: The magnetic force on a charge moving through a uniform field is greatest when the angle between its velocity and the field is:
questions.x: F = qvB sin θ is largest when sin θ = 1, at θ = 90°. At 0° and 180° the force is zero.

questions.q: The flux through a coil whose ends are not connected to anything is changing. Which statement is correct?
o: An emf is induced, but no current flows
A current flows, but no emf is induced
Neither an emf nor a current is produced
Both an emf and a current are produced
questions.x: Faraday's law gives an emf whenever the flux linking the coil changes. A current needs a closed circuit, so with open ends no current flows.

questions.q: A steady current in coil P is suddenly switched off. In a nearby coaxial coil Q, a brief induced current flows:
o: In the opposite sense to the current that was in P
In both senses equally, so the net current is zero
In the same sense as the current that was in P
Only if Q is connected to a battery
questions.x: The flux through Q falls. By Lenz's law the induced current tries to keep that flux, so it flows in the same sense as P's former current.

questions.q: Keeping the supply voltage fixed, the frequency applied to an ideal coil is raised to twice its value. The current it carries:
questions.x: XL = 2πfL, so doubling f doubles the reactance. With fixed voltage, I = V/XL falls to half.

questions.q: In a working half-wave rectifier, the diode is taken out and put back the other way round. The output across the load now:
o: Is still half-wave DC, but of opposite polarity, using the other half-cycle
Becomes zero for the whole cycle
questions.x: The reversed diode conducts during the other half of the input cycle, so the load still gets one pulse per cycle but with the current in the opposite direction.

questions.q: Light above the threshold frequency is switched on and falls on a metal. Photoelectrons are observed:
o: Only after the metal has absorbed energy for several minutes
Only after the metal becomes hot
After a delay that is longer for brighter light
Practically instantly, with no measurable delay
questions.x: Each electron absorbs a whole photon in a single event, so emission starts at once. A delay would be expected only if energy built up gradually, as in the wave picture.

questions.q: Samples of isotopes X (half-life 2 h) and Y (half-life 4 h) start with equal numbers of undecayed nuclei. After 8 hours, the ratio of undecayed X nuclei to undecayed Y nuclei is:
questions.x: X has gone through 4 half-lives (1/16 left) and Y through 2 (1/4 left). Ratio = (1/16) : (1/4) = 1 : 4.

questions.q: By how many neutrons does a nucleus of uranium-238 differ from a nucleus of uranium-235?
questions.x: Both have Z = 92, so the difference in mass number, 238 − 235 = 3, is all neutrons. U-235 itself has 143 neutrons.

questions.q: The college's annual sports day will be held on 15 March. Students who wish to take part must give their names to Mr Khalid by 1 March. No student may enter more than two events. The races will begin at 8:30 a.m., and prizes will be given at 1 p.m. by the chief guest. According to the notice, by what date must students give their names?
questions.x: Names must reach Mr Khalid by 1 March. The 15th of March is the date of the sports day itself.

questions.q: Choose the correct pair: "Ali has lived in Quetta ___ 2018 and has taught at the same school ___ six years."
questions.x: 'Since' marks a starting point (2018) and 'for' marks a length of time (six years).

questions.q: Which sentence uses 'still' and 'yet' in their correct positions?
o: Ali is yet waiting, but the bus has not come still.
Ali is waiting yet, but the bus still has come.
Ali is still waiting, but the bus has not come yet.
Ali still is waiting yet, but the bus has come not.
questions.x: 'Still' goes before the main verb for a continuing action, and 'yet' goes at the end of a negative sentence.

questions.q: In "Ali came to the laboratory to collect his results", the infinitive phrase 'to collect his results' tells us:
questions.x: An infinitive after a verb of action often shows purpose; it answers 'why did he come?'

questions.q: "Rather than being candid about his poor marks, Bilal hid his report card and changed the subject whenever his father asked." The word 'candid' means:
questions.x: 'Candid' means open and truthful; 'rather than' tells us Bilal did the opposite of being candid by hiding the truth.

questions.q: Choose the correct relative pronoun: "The scientist ___ discovered penicillin was Alexander Fleming."
questions.x: The antecedent is a person and the pronoun is the subject of 'discovered', so 'who' is correct; 'whom' is used for objects.

questions.q: Choose the correct preposition: "In the evening we walked slowly ___ the river bank, enjoying the breeze."
questions.x: 'Along' shows movement following the length of something, such as a river bank.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "I am looking forward to meet you at the conference."
o: I am looking forward for meeting you at the conference.
I am looking forward to meeting you at the conference.
I am looking forward to met you at the conference.
I am looking forward meet you at the conference.
questions.x: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by an -ing form: 'looking forward to meeting'.

questions.q: In which sentence does the verb agree with its subject?
o: The scissors is on the table.
The scissors are on the table.
Your glasses is on the desk.
questions.x: Nouns for things made of two matching parts, such as scissors, glasses and trousers, are plural and take plural verbs: 'the scissors are'.

questions.q: Which belief is based on evidence rather than being a false belief?
o: A black cat crossing your path brings bad luck
Washing hands with soap reduces the spread of germs
Wearing a lucky ring raises exam marks
Breaking a mirror causes years of misfortune
questions.x: Handwashing with soap removing germs is shown by experiments and observation. The other three have no known cause-and-effect link and are superstitions.

questions.q: A fair coin has landed heads five times in a row. Fatima believes the next toss is more likely to be tails. Why is her belief false?
o: Each toss is independent, so the chance of tails is still one half
After five heads, heads becomes more likely
A coin cannot land heads five times in a row
Tails becomes certain after five heads
questions.x: A fair coin has no memory: earlier tosses do not change the next result. The chance stays one half for heads and one half for tails.

questions.q: Find the next number: 60, 54, 49, 45, 42, ?
questions.x: The amounts subtracted fall by one each time: -6, -5, -4, -3, so next is -2: 42 - 2 = 40.

questions.q: Six exams, Biology, Chemistry, English, Logic, Physics and Urdu, are held one per day from Monday to Saturday. Chemistry is on Thursday. Physics is two days before Chemistry, and Biology the day after Physics. English is not on Monday. Urdu is after Chemistry. Which exam is on Monday?
questions.x: Physics is Tuesday and Biology Wednesday. Monday, Friday and Saturday remain; English cannot be Monday and Urdu must be after Thursday, so Logic is on Monday.

questions.q: When a number is doubled and 5 is added, the result is 29. If the same number is then divided by 3, what is the result?
questions.x: 2n + 5 = 29 gives n = 12. Then 12 divided by 3 = 4.

questions.q: Statement: Many dead fish were found in a lake near a town, and a factory upstream was recently seen draining waste into the stream that feeds the lake. Courses of action: I. The factory's waste should be tested, and the factory stopped from releasing untreated waste if it is the source. II. Fishing in the lake should be suspended until tests show the water is safe. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Action I checks and controls the likely source. Action II is a sensible temporary step to protect people until the water is proven safe. Both are practical.

questions.q: Statement: A student got low marks in biology because he studied only from short notes and skipped the textbook. Courses of action: I. He should drop biology as a subject. II. He should study from the textbook along with his notes. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: The cause is skipping the textbook, so adding it to his study fixes the problem. Dropping the subject is an extreme reaction.

questions.q: A shopkeeper's shop was badly damaged in a flood. He says, "Everything is lost; there is no point in starting again." Which is the strongest argument to encourage him?
o: He still has his skills and his customers' trust, which he can use to rebuild step by step
Floods never happen twice in the same place
He should wait for his luck to change by itself
Other shopkeepers lost even more than he did
questions.x: His skills and reputation are real resources that make rebuilding possible. The other replies rely on false claims, luck or comparison rather than a reason to act.

questions.q: Statement I: More girls from a district joined medical colleges this year. Statement II: Two years ago, a free science coaching centre for girls opened in the district. Which of the following is correct?
o: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Both statements are effects of some common cause
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both statements are effects of independent causes
questions.x: The coaching began two years earlier, giving students time to prepare. Better preparation then led to more admissions, so the centre is the cause.
